sections.normalized_html:

[MATH: x=1-t, \quad y= \dfrac{2}{3} t^{3/2}, \qquad t\in[0,1].]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/c85ca457e7f02850924980f54ba585bf]

Find an integral expression for the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

[MATH: x=1-t, \quad y= \dfrac{2}{3} t^{3/2}, \qquad t\in[0,1].]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To compute the arc length [MATH: L] of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

[MATH: L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.]

Computing the derivatives of [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we have

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(1 − t) = − 1]

and

[MATH: (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)((2)/(3)t^{3/2}) = t^{1/2}.]

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

[MATH: L|= ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}sqrt((− 1)^{2} + (t^{1/2})^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}sqrt(1 + t)dt.]

To compute the arc length [MATH: L] of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

[MATH: L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.]

Computing the derivatives of [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we have

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(1 − t) = − 1]

and

[MATH: (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)((2)/(3)t^{3/2}) = t^{1/2}.]

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

[MATH: L|= ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}sqrt((− 1)^{2} + (t^{1/2})^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}sqrt(1 + t)dt.]

sections.normalized_html:
Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

[MATH: x=e^t(\cos{t}+\sin{t}), \quad y=e^t(\cos{t}-\sin{t}) , \quad t\in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right].]
sections.readable_text:
Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

[MATH: x=e^t(\cos{t}+\sin{t}), \quad y=e^t(\cos{t}-\sin{t}) , \quad t\in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right].]

[IMG: /graphics/01cb59beb0b1df4a0cf0402429bafa19]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Computing the derivatives of [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we have

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(e^{t}(\cos t + \sin t)); = e^{t}(\cos t + \sin t) + e^{t}(− \sin t + \cos t); = 2e^{t}\cos t]

and

[MATH: (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(e^{t}(\cos t − \sin t)); = e^{t}(\cos t − \sin t) + e^{t}(− \sin t − \cos t); = − 2e^{t}\sin t.]

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

[MATH: L|= ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/4}sqrt((2e^{t}\cos t)^{2} + (− 2e^{t}\sin t)^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/4}sqrt(4e^{2t}(\cos^{2} t + \sin^{2} t))dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/4}2e^{t}dt; = 2e^{t}|_{0}^{π/4}; = 2(e^{π/4} − 1).]

[MATH: (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(e^{t}(\cos t − \sin t)); = e^{t}(\cos t − \sin t) + e^{t}(− \sin t − \cos t); = − 2e^{t}\sin t.]

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

Let's go back to our first example, which was to find the arc length of the curve defined by

Content:
[MATH: x=2\cos{t}, \quad y=2\sin{t}, \quad t\in\left[ 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right].]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b1e3cd196df295e05a912b4b43882b5b]

Content:
First, we divide the interval [MATH: \left[ 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right]] into small subintervals of equal length. Consider a part of the blue arc that corresponds to one of those subintervals and let the length of that part be [MATH: \Delta{s}].

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/27415db192d1ddfa89ddc350a95f12fd]

Content:
We can now denote the horizontal displacement as [MATH: \Delta{x}] and the vertical shift as [MATH: \Delta{y}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/484bdaf55d0db351802a45758c78cf15]

Content:
To approximate the length [MATH: \Delta{s}] we apply the Pythagorean theorem, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: Δs|≈ sqrt((Δx)^{2} + (Δy)^{2}).]
To approximate the total length [MATH: L,] we need to sum up all of the little [MATH: \Delta s] terms, so

Content:
[MATH: L \approx \sum \Delta s = \sum \sqrt{\left( \Delta{x} \right)^2 + \left( \Delta{y} \right)^2}.]

Content:
We then take the limit as [MATH: \Delta x, \Delta y \rightarrow 0.] As we do this, the sum becomes a definite integral, and our approximation approaches the exact value of [MATH: L]. So, using the chain rule, we arrive at

Content:
[MATH: L|= ∫sqrt((dx)^{2} + (dy)^{2}); = ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}sqrt(((dx)/(dt) ⋅ dt)^{2} + ((dy)/(dt) ⋅ dt)^{2}); = ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} ⋅ (dt)^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2} ⋅ (dt)^{2}); = ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2}) ⋅ sqrt(dt^{2}); = ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2})dt.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we would like to find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

Content:
[MATH: x=2\cos{t}, \quad y=2\sin{t}]

Content:
from [MATH: t=0] to [MATH: t=\dfrac{\pi}{2},] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fba5b3189129d2cee312509b6ce706a1]

Content:
It can be shown that the arc length [MATH: L] of a curve defined parametrically by
[MATH: x=x(t), \quad y=y(t), \qquad t\in [t_1,t_2],]

Content:
is given by the formula

Content:
[MATH: L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\textrm{d}t.]

Content:
The intuition behind this formula is given at the end of this tutorial.

Content:
According to the formula, the length of the blue arc is

Content:
[MATH: L|= ∫_{0}^{π/2}sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/2}sqrt(((d)/(dt)(2\cos t))^{2} + ((d)/(dt)(2\sin t))^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/2}sqrt((− 2\sin t)^{2} + (2\cos t)^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/2}sqrt(4(\sin^{2} t + \cos^{2} t))dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/2}2dt; = 2t|_{0}^{π/2}; = 2((π)/(2) − 0); = π.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/c85ca457e7f02850924980f54ba585bf]

Find an integral expression for the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

[MATH: x=1-t, \quad y= \dfrac{2}{3} t^{3/2}, \qquad t\in[0,1].]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To compute the arc length [MATH: L] of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

[MATH: L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.]

Computing the derivatives of [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we have

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(1 − t) = − 1]

and

[MATH: (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)((2)/(3)t^{3/2}) = t^{1/2}.]

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

[MATH: L|= ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}sqrt((− 1)^{2} + (t^{1/2})^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}sqrt(1 + t)dt.]

---

Item 5 — Example: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions

Example Prompt:
Find the expression that gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
[MATH: x=t, \, y=\ln{(\cos{t})}]
from [MATH: t=0] to [MATH: t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}] (see graph below).

[IMG: /graphics/f10352be16212d467425c8695c797467]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To compute the arc length [MATH: L] of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

[MATH: L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.]

Computing the derivatives of [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we have
[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(t) = 1]
and
[MATH: (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(\ln (\cos t)) = − \tan t.]

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get
[MATH: L|= ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/4}sqrt((1)^{2} + (− \tan t)^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/4}sqrt(1 + \tan^{2} t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/4}sqrt(\sec^{2} t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/4}\sec tdt.]

---

Item 8 — Example: Finding the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve

Example Prompt:
Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

[MATH: x=e^t(\cos{t}+\sin{t}), \quad y=e^t(\cos{t}-\sin{t}) , \quad t\in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right].]

[IMG: /graphics/01cb59beb0b1df4a0cf0402429bafa19]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Computing the derivatives of [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we have

[MATH: (dx)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(e^{t}(\cos t + \sin t)); = e^{t}(\cos t + \sin t) + e^{t}(− \sin t + \cos t); = 2e^{t}\cos t]

and

[MATH: (dy)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)(e^{t}(\cos t − \sin t)); = e^{t}(\cos t − \sin t) + e^{t}(− \sin t − \cos t); = − 2e^{t}\sin t.]

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

[MATH: L|= ∫_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/4}sqrt((2e^{t}\cos t)^{2} + (− 2e^{t}\sin t)^{2})dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/4}sqrt(4e^{2t}(\cos^{2} t + \sin^{2} t))dt; = ∫_{0}^{π/4}2e^{t}dt; = 2e^{t}|_{0}^{π/4}; = 2(e^{π/4} − 1).]

---
